## Contagion by invisible living agents (germ theory) `contagion_theory`
- Deps: helped by microscope, microorganisms, spontaneous_generation_refuted, natural_causes
- Core idea: Many diseases are caused by living things too small to see, which multiply in the body and pass to the next person by specific routes: excrement in water and food, unwashed hands, coughing, wounds, and biting insects (fleas, lice, mosquitoes). Different agents may cause similar illnesses, and some have several routes, so the defence differs: clean water against cholera, delousing against typhus, clean hands against childbed fever. Not bad air (miasma), not the stars, not an imbalance of humours. The most convincing argument without a microscope is practical: block one route and compare deaths between exposed and less-exposed groups or before and after an intervention (Semmelweis's two wards, Snow's two water companies). Koch's historical criteria for causal evidence were: find the germ in every case, grow it pure, produce the disease with it in an animal, and recover it again. Some infections do not meet all these criteria.
- Pitfalls: Claiming all diseases are caused by germs (scurvy, rickets, pellagra, goitre, cancer and many others are not) | Saying 'tiny animals cause disease' without naming the route, so nobody knows what to do differently | Assuming every disease spreads through the air or by touch; bubonic plague, malaria and epidemic typhus commonly involve insect vectors, while pneumonic plague can spread between people, cholera needs swallowed excrement | Dismissing miasma measures entirely: draining swamps and removing filth did work, for the wrong reason | Believing that seeing microbes proves they cause disease; healthy people are full of harmless ones
- History: rome: c. 37 BC – Varro warns of invisible tiny animals from marshes entering through mouth and nose (De re rustica I.12); a guess with no consequences; islamic: c. 1349–1362 – Ibn al-Khatib and Ibn Khatima (Granada) argue from observation that plague passes by contact, clothes and vessels; china: 1642 – Wu Youxing, Wenyi lun, says epidemics come from specific pestilential agents entering by mouth and nose, not from weather; europe: 1546 – Fracastoro, seeds of contagion; 1835 Bassi shows a fungus causes a silkworm disease; 1840 Henle; 1860s Pasteur; 1876 Koch proves anthrax, 1882 tuberculosis; Koch's postulates stated 1884–1890
- Read: Girolamo Fracastoro, De contagione et contagiosis morbis et eorum curatione (1546) | Robert Koch, Die Aetiologie der Tuberculose, Berliner klinische Wochenschrift (1882) | Paul de Kruif, Microbe Hunters (1926)

## Abandoning bloodletting, purging and mercury (end of humoral medicine) `bloodletting_harm`
- Deps: helped by controlled_trial, empiricism_over_authority, blood_circulation, placebo_blinding
- Core idea: The standard treatments of learned medicine from Galen to the 1850s (opening a vein, purging, forced vomiting, blistering, mercury salts) rest on the theory of four humours and weaken the patient; in fevers, diarrhoea, childbirth and after wounds they kill. A sick person needs rest, water, food, warmth and cleanliness. The treatments seemed to work because most illnesses get better by themselves and the doctor took the credit. In Paris, Pierre Louis compared pneumonia patients bled early with those bled later. Mortality was higher in the early group, but the groups differed in age and had been selected by the course of their illness.
- Pitfalls: Attacking the physicians head-on without numbers; they have 1,500 years of authority and the patient's own expectations on their side | Throwing out the remedies that do work with the theory: opium, cinchona bark, willow bark, setting bones, lancing abscesses | Replacing bleeding with another untested cure of one's own | Thinking only Europe did this: bloodletting and purging were also standard in Indian, Islamic and Mesoamerican medicine
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – Hippocratic writings; humoral theory with a cautious, mostly dietary therapy; rome: 2nd c. AD – Galen makes bloodletting a universal remedy; india: early centuries AD – Sushruta Samhita describes venesection and leeches (dating of the text disputed); islamic: 9th–11th c. – venesection (fasd) and cupping (hijama) systematised by al-Razi and Ibn Sina; europe: 1648 – van Helmont proposes a trial by lot of bleeding against no bleeding (never held); 1799 George Washington dies after losing about 2.4 litres of blood in a day; 1835 Pierre Louis's numerical method shows little benefit; abandoned c. 1850–1900
- Read: Pierre-Charles-Alexandre Louis, Recherches sur les effets de la saignée dans quelques maladies inflammatoires (1835) | David Wootton, Bad Medicine: Doctors Doing Harm Since Hippocrates (2006)

## Counting and mapping cases to find causes (epidemiology) `epidemiology_mapping`
- Deps: helped by probability_statistics, census_vital_registration, data_graphs, correlation_causation_confounding, public_health_board
- Core idea: To find the cause of an outbreak, define what counts as a case, then record every case by time (when it began), place (house, street, water source) and person (age, trade, what they ate and drank). Divide cases by the number of people exposed to get rates, and compare the rate among those who shared a suspected cause with those who did not. Mark cases on a map and look hardest at the exceptions: in 1854 the brewery men near the Broad Street pump drank beer and stayed well, while a widow miles away who had the pump water sent to her died.
- Pitfalls: Comparing raw counts without the number of people at risk (a large parish always has more deaths) | Taking a pattern for a cause: William Farr's cholera deaths followed elevation above the Thames neatly, and the cause was still the water | Believing a map alone proves anything; Snow's argument rested on rates and exceptions, the map was drawn afterwards | Collecting only cases that fit the theory
- History: europe: 1452 – Milan keeps continuous death registers with causes; 1662 Graunt analyses the London bills of mortality; 1835 Louis's numerical method; 1839 Farr at the General Register Office; 1846 Panum on measles in the Faroes; 1854–1855 Snow on cholera; 1950 Doll and Hill link tobacco smoking to lung cancer in a British case-control study; americas: 1798 – Seaman maps yellow fever in New York; 1914–1915 Goldberger shows by diet studies in orphanages and prisons that pellagra is not an infection
- Read: John Graunt, Natural and Political Observations Made upon the Bills of Mortality (1662) | John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (2nd ed., 1855) | Alfredo Morabia (ed.), A History of Epidemiologic Methods and Concepts (2004)

## Hand washing with soap `hand_hygiene`
- Deps: needs soap; helped by contagion_theory, chlorine_bleach, controlled_trial
- Core idea: Hands carry disease from excrement, corpses, pus and the sick to mouths, food, wounds and women in labour. Wet the hands, rub soap over every surface for about 20 seconds (backs, between the fingers, thumbs, under short-cut nails), rinse under poured or running water, not in a shared basin, and dry on a clean cloth or in the air. Always after defecating or cleaning a child, before preparing food and eating, before and after touching a wound, a patient or a birth, and after touching the dead. Surgery calls for surgical hand antisepsis before sterile gloves. Chlorinated lime was a historical intervention: in Semmelweis's Vienna clinic, deaths of mothers fell from about one in ten to about one in a hundred once students washed in chlorinated lime after autopsies.
- Pitfalls: A quick rinse in water, or in a basin everyone shares, which spreads the dirt around | Thinking only visible dirt or bad smell matters; Semmelweis's students had hands that looked clean | Washing only after the work instead of before touching the patient or the food | Drying on a dirty common towel or apron | Assuming gloves replace hand hygiene; hands can be contaminated while removing them
- History: india: early centuries AD – Sushruta Samhita asks the surgeon to be clean with short nails and hair (dating disputed); islamic: 7th c. onward – ritual washing before prayer and meals makes frequent washing habitual, without soap or a disease theory; europe: 1795 – Gordon (Aberdeen) shows childbed fever is carried by attendants; 1847 Semmelweis introduces chlorinated-lime hand washing in Vienna: first clinic mortality about 11 % in 1846, about 1.3 % in 1848; americas: 1843 – Oliver Wendell Holmes argues in Boston that attendants can carry childbed fever; global: 2005 – trial in Karachi squatter settlements: soap and hand-washing promotion halves childhood diarrhoea and pneumonia
- Read: Ignaz Semmelweis, Die Aetiologie, der Begriff und die Prophylaxis des Kindbettfiebers (1861) | Sherwin B. Nuland, The Doctors' Plague (2003) | Stephen P. Luby et al., Effect of handwashing on child health: a randomised controlled trial, The Lancet (2005)

## Boiling drinking water and protecting wells `boiled_water`
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, cholera_waterborne, water_filtration_chlorination
- Core idea: Water that looks, smells and tastes clean can carry cholera, typhoid and dysentery if excrement has reached it. Bringing it to a full rolling boil for a minute (three minutes high in the mountains) makes it safe; let cloudy water settle or strain it through cloth first. Keep boiled water in a covered, narrow-necked vessel and pour it out; never dip cups or hands in. Protect the source as well: line the well, give it a raised rim, a cover and its own clean bucket, drain spilt water away, and keep latrines, dung heaps and graves about 30 m away and downhill. Take river water upstream of the town.
- Pitfalls: Trusting clear, cool or running water; 'a stream cleans itself after a few yards' is false | Boiling and then dirtying the water again with a dipped cup, dirty hands or an open jar | Believing boiling removes poisons; lead, arsenic and salt stay and become more concentrated | Thinking the alcohol in weak beer or watered wine makes it safe; beer is safe because the wort was boiled, and the story that medieval people drank only beer because water was deadly is a myth | Only warming the water instead of bringing it to the boil
- History: greece: c. 400 BC – Hippocratic Airs, Waters, Places judges health by the water and advises boiling and straining some waters; rome: 1st c. AD – Pliny records boiled drinking water (Nero's decocta); aqueducts bring spring water from outside the city; india: early centuries AD – Sushruta Samhita discusses boiling water and clarifying turbid water, including with cloth (dating disputed); china: from c. 8th c. (Tang) – tea drinking makes boiled water habitual; the health benefit is plausible but was never measured; europe: 1854 – Snow traces cholera to the Broad Street pump; 1880s Koch's bacteriology explains why boiling works
- Read: Steven Johnson, The Ghost Map (2006) | M. N. Baker, The Quest for Pure Water (1948) | World Health Organization, Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (4th ed., 2011)

## Slow sand filtration and chlorination of town water `water_filtration_chlorination`
- Deps: helped by chlorine_bleach, cholera_waterborne, contagion_theory
- Core idea: A town can treat its water centrally. Let the water stand in a settling basin, then run it slowly downwards (10–30 cm of water depth per hour) through a bed of fine sand about a metre deep resting on gravel and drain pipes. After one to three weeks a slimy living layer grows on the sand surface and removes almost all germs; the bed must stay wet and running, and is cleaned by scraping off the top centimetre. Chlorine demand varies. For clear water below pH 8, check that at least 0.5 mg/L of free chlorine remains after at least 30 minutes of contact. Some parasites resist ordinary chlorination, so filtration still matters. Hamburg, which drank unfiltered Elbe water, lost about 8,600 people to cholera in 1892; Altona next door, with sand filters, was nearly spared.
- Pitfalls: Filtering fast through coarse sand or cloth, which clears the water but leaves the germs | Letting the filter run dry or scraping away the whole living layer and using the water at once | Thinking charcoal makes water safe; it removes taste and smell, not disease | Dosing chlorine by guess: too little does nothing, far too much is undrinkable; muddy water uses the chlorine up | Placing the intake downstream of the town's own sewers
- History: india: early centuries AD – the Sushruta Samhita describes clarifying turbid water with materials including cloth and kataka seeds (dating disputed); europe: 1804 – Gibb's sand filter, Paisley; 1829 Simpson's slow sand filters, Chelsea Waterworks, London; 1852 filtration required for London's river water; 1892 Hamburg and Altona; 1897 emergency chlorination at Maidstone; 1902 continuous chlorination at Middelkerke, Belgium; americas: 1908 – Jersey City (Leal and Fuller) chlorinates a whole city supply; typhoid in American cities collapses within a decade
- Read: M. N. Baker, The Quest for Pure Water (1948) | L. Huisman and W. E. Wood, Slow Sand Filtration (World Health Organization, 1974) | Michael J. McGuire, The Chlorine Revolution (2013)

## Latrines and sewers (keeping excrement out of water, food and soil) `sanitation_sewerage`
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, cholera_waterborne, public_health_board, fired_brick_ceramics
- Core idea: Most deadly diarrhoeal diseases and worms travel from one person's excrement to another's mouth through water, hands, flies, soil and crops. Every household needs a pit latrine: a pit two or three metres deep whose bottom stays at least 1.5 m above the groundwater, about 30 m from any well and downhill of it, with a slab, a tight lid or a vent pipe against flies, and a place to wash hands next to it. Cover a full pit with earth and dig a new one. Night soil for the fields must undergo treatment verified to destroy persistent worm eggs. In towns, closed sewers must carry waste to a point downstream of every water intake; a water-seal bend (S-trap) under each drain keeps the gas and the rats out of the house.
- Pitfalls: Building sewers that empty into the river above the water intake; London's cholera got worse after cesspools were flushed into the Thames in the 1840s | Digging the latrine next to or uphill of the well, or down to the groundwater | Fighting the smell (perfume, lime on top, burning herbs) instead of the contact with excrement | Spreading fresh night soil on vegetables; roundworm eggs survive for months | Assuming Roman-style baths and public latrines made people healthy; shared sponges and warm unchanged bath water did not, and Roman-era remains show as many intestinal parasites as before
- History: mesopotamia: c. 3000–2500 BC – clay drain pipes and brick-lined latrines over cesspits (e.g. Eshnunna); india: c. 2600–1900 BC – Indus cities (Mohenjo-daro, Harappa): house latrines and bathrooms connected to covered brick street drains; greece: c. 1700 BC – Minoan Knossos: stone drains and a latrine flushed with water; rome: c. 6th c. BC – Cloaca Maxima begun as a drainage channel (traditional date); imperial public latrines and sewers, mainly for drainage and convenience; china: Han period (206 BC – AD 220) – latrines built over pigsties; organised collection of night soil as fertiliser in later cities; europe: 1596 – Harington's flushing closet; 1775 Cumming patents the S-trap; 1842 Chadwick's sanitary report; 1859–1875 Bazalgette's intercepting sewers for London
- Read: Edwin Chadwick, Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population of Great Britain (1842) | E. G. Wagner and J. N. Lanoix, Excreta Disposal for Rural Areas and Small Communities (World Health Organization, 1958) | Stephen Halliday, The Great Stink of London (1999)

## Food hygiene (cooking, flies, carriers) `food_hygiene`
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, hand_hygiene, boiled_water, pasteurisation, refrigeration
- Core idea: Food carries disease when excrement reaches it on hands, flies or dirty water, and when germs multiply in it while it stands warm. Five rules cover most of it: wash hands and tools; keep raw meat and its juices away from cooked food; cook meat, eggs and reheated dishes until they are steaming hot all the way through; eat food soon after cooking or keep it cold or boiling hot, not lukewarm for hours; use clean water and wash or peel raw fruit and vegetables. Cover food and latrines against flies. A healthy-looking cook can carry typhoid for years, so nobody with diarrhoea handles food and cooks wash their hands above all others. Boil milk.
- Pitfalls: Trusting smell and taste; dangerous food usually smells normal | Believing salt, spices, smoke or a splash of vinegar make spoiled meat safe | Keeping cooked food lukewarm overnight; reheating may leave toxins already formed in the food | Blaming the food itself (fruit, cucumbers, fish) for epidemics instead of what got onto it
- History: china: long-standing custom of eating food cooked and hot and drinking boiled water; a habit, not a theory; europe: 1820–1822 – Kerner describes sausage poisoning (botulism); 1888 Gaertner isolates a bacterium from a meat poisoning outbreak; 1895 van Ermengem finds the botulism bacterium; americas: 1898 – US Army Typhoid Board (Reed, Vaughan, Shakespeare) blames flies and soiled hands in camps; 1907 Soper traces household outbreaks to the healthy cook Mary Mallon
- Read: World Health Organization, Five Keys to Safer Food Manual (2006) | George A. Soper, The work of a chronic typhoid germ distributor, Journal of the American Medical Association (1907) | Judith Walzer Leavitt, Typhoid Mary: Captive to the Public's Health (1996)

## Quarantine and isolation of the sick `quarantine`
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, public_health_board, plague_vectors
- Core idea: Two different measures. Isolation: a person who is sick with a catching disease is nursed apart, in a separate room or house, by one attendant (best someone who has already survived the disease), with their own dishes, and their bedding and clothes are boiled or burnt. Quarantine: healthy people, ships and goods coming from an infected place are kept apart and watched for longer than the disease takes to show itself (a week for plague, three weeks for smallpox), then let in if nobody has fallen ill. Both need food and wages delivered to those shut in, or people hide cases and flee. It works for diseases passed between people; it does little against cholera in the water or plague rats that walk past the guards.
- Pitfalls: Shutting the healthy family in the house with the sick, as in London in 1665; it kills them and makes people conceal illness | Treating forty days as magic; the right length follows from how long the disease takes to appear | Exemptions for the rich, for merchants and for the army, which is how epidemics get through | Fumigating letters and goods while ignoring rats, fleas, lice and water | Isolating the sick without feeding and nursing them, which turns the lazaretto into a death house
- History: china: c. 217 BC – Qin legal texts from Shuihudi appear to order lepers moved to a separate place (reading debated); 1910–1911 Wu Lien-teh leads isolation, travel-control and masking measures during the Manchurian plague epidemic; islamic: 7th c. – tradition ascribed to Muhammad: do not enter or leave a land with plague; 707 leper house founded in Damascus under al-Walid I; europe: 1348 – Milan and other cities bar the infected; 1377 Ragusa (Dubrovnik) orders 30 days of isolation for arrivals, later 40; 1423 Venice opens the first permanent plague hospital (Lazzaretto Vecchio)
- Read: Carlo M. Cipolla, Public Health and the Medical Profession in the Renaissance (1976) | Zlata Blažina Tomić and Vesna Blažina, Expelling the Plague: The Health Office and the Implementation of Quarantine in Dubrovnik, 1377–1533 (2015)

## Hospital hygiene and trained nursing `nursing_hospital_hygiene`
- Deps: helped by hand_hygiene, sanitation_sewerage, data_graphs, contagion_theory
- Core idea: A hospital that crowds the sick together kills more than it cures unless it is run for cleanliness. One patient per bed with space between beds; windows that open; clean water and working drains; bedding and bandages boiled between patients; patients washed and fed properly; excrement and soiled dressings carried out and burnt or buried; fever, wound and childbirth cases in separate rooms with separate attendants. Nurses are trained, paid and sober, wash their hands between patients and keep written records. Count admissions and deaths by cause every month in the same way, so wards and hospitals can be compared and a change that works can be proved.
- Pitfalls: Crediting kindness and scrubbing alone: deaths at Scutari fell only after the Sanitary Commission flushed the sewers and opened the ventilation in spring 1855 | Explaining it by bad air; Nightingale herself did, and long doubted germs, yet the measures worked | Reusing one sponge, one basin and one probe from bed to bed | Building one huge hospital for all the sick of a city without separating fevers from wounds and births
- History: rome: 1st c. AD – legionary hospitals (valetudinaria) with separate small rooms; india: 3rd c. BC – Ashoka's edicts provide medical care for people and animals; 9th c. monastic hospital at Mihintale (Sri Lanka); islamic: 9th c. – bimaristans in Baghdad; 872 Ibn Tulun hospital, Cairo; 1284 Mansuri hospital, Cairo, with separate wards by disease, salaried staff and a pharmacy; europe: c. 370 – Basil's hospital at Caesarea; 1288 Santa Maria Nuova, Florence; 1788 Tenon exposes the Hôtel-Dieu in Paris with several patients per bed; 1854–1856 Nightingale at Scutari; 1860 nursing school at St Thomas's, London
- Read: Florence Nightingale, Notes on Hospitals (3rd ed., 1863) | Florence Nightingale, Notes on Nursing: What It Is, and What It Is Not (1859) | Hugh Small, Florence Nightingale: Avenging Angel (1998)

## Cholera and typhoid spread through drinking water `cholera_waterborne`
- Deps: helped by epidemiology_mapping, contagion_theory, boiled_water, microscope
- Core idea: Cholera, typhoid and dysentery are swallowed: the excrement of the sick gets into wells and rivers and onto hands and food, and swallowing contaminated food or water may cause infection, sometimes without symptoms. Smell does not matter; men working in the sewers were not struck more than others. The proof is Snow's comparison of two London water companies supplying the same streets in 1854: houses served with sewage-tainted Thames water had 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 houses, houses served from above the city had 37. So: close or boil suspect sources, move intakes upstream, keep latrines away from wells, and wash hands after nursing the sick. Fluid loss is the immediate danger. Oral rehydration treats most cases; severe dehydration requires urgent intravenous fluid as well.
- Pitfalls: Telling the pump-handle story as the proof; the outbreak was already fading and the map came later, the water-company comparison is the strong evidence | Treating cholera with bleeding, calomel or by withholding water, the usual treatments, which kill | Believing clear water from a deep-looking well is safe; the Broad Street well was fouled by a cesspit a metre away | Mixing up typhoid (water, food, carriers) with typhus (lice) | Expecting Asiatic cholera in Europe before 1830; the word 'cholera' in older texts means ordinary vomiting and diarrhoea
- History: india: 1817 – first pandemic spreads from Bengal, where cholera was long endemic; 1884 Koch identifies the bacterium in Calcutta; europe: 1831 – cholera reaches western Europe; 1849 and 1855 Snow's water theory; 1854 Pacini sees the vibrio in Florence (ignored); 1856–1873 Budd on typhoid; 1892 Hamburg epidemic settles the dispute; americas: 1832 – cholera reaches North America
- Read: John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (2nd ed., 1855) | Steven Johnson, The Ghost Map (2006) | Sandra Hempel, The Medical Detective: John Snow, Cholera and the Mystery of the Broad Street Pump (2006)

## Oral rehydration (water, salt and sugar) `oral_rehydration`
- Deps: helped by boiled_water, cholera_waterborne
- Core idea: Diarrhoea can cause fatal loss of water and salts within hours. The gut can still absorb sodium together with glucose, and water follows. Mix a standard oral rehydration salts packet with the exact volume of safe water specified. If no packet is available, the emergency household mixture is six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt in one litre of safe water. Offer frequent small sips, replace ongoing stool losses and continue feeding and breastfeeding. Shock, severe dehydration or inability to drink requires urgent medical care and intravenous fluids.
- Pitfalls: Too much salt, which can kill a child; use level measures and remake a mixture of uncertain strength | Withholding drink and food to 'rest the bowel', the traditional and deadly advice | Giving plain water only, or sugary drinks without salt | Honey for babies under one year (risk of botulism) | Stopping when the patient vomits instead of giving smaller sips more often
- History: india: 1953 – H. N. Chatterjee, Calcutta, treats cholera with an oral glucose and salt solution; 1971 Dilip Mahalanabis uses it in refugee camps of the Bangladesh war and reports a case fatality of about 4 % among the patients treated; europe: 1832 – Latta in Scotland revives cholera patients with salt water into a vein, forgotten again; global: 1960 – Crane describes the coupled uptake of sodium and glucose; 1968 trials in Dhaka (Nalin, Cash) and Calcutta (Pierce) show the drink can replace infusions; 1978 adopted by WHO
- Read: David R. Nalin, Richard A. Cash et al., Oral maintenance therapy for cholera in adults, The Lancet (1968) | Joshua Nalibow Ruxin, Magic bullet: the history of oral rehydration therapy, Medical History (1994) | World Health Organization, Oral Rehydration Salts: Production of the New ORS (2006)

## Plague carried by rats and fleas (and by coughing) `plague_vectors`
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, quarantine, microscope
- Core idea: Plague is a disease of rats and other rodents. When the rats die, their fleas move to people and inject the disease with their bite; swollen glands (buboes) follow in two to six days. If it reaches the lungs it passes straight from person to person by coughing and kills within days. Dead rats in the houses are the warning sign. Measures: store grain so rats cannot reach it, kill fleas in clothes and bedding by boiling or baking, keep people out of houses where rats have died, isolate the sick, and cover mouth and nose with layers of cloth when nursing patients who cough blood. Clothes and bales can carry fleas a long way.
- Pitfalls: Saying rats bite people or that the rat itself is the danger; killing rats without killing fleas drives hungry fleas onto humans | Blaming or protecting cats and dogs; the story that killing cats caused the Black Death is a legend | Treating all plague as airborne, or none of it; bubonic and pneumonic forms need different defences | Lancing buboes, bleeding the patient, or relying on perfumes and beak masks | Overstating certainty for the Black Death: some researchers argue human fleas and body lice spread it between people, which would make delousing as important as rat control
- History: china: 1894 – Yersin (and, less clearly, Kitasato) find the bacterium in Hong Kong; 1910–1911 Wu Lien-teh recognises airborne pneumonic plague in Manchuria and introduces masks; east_asia: 1897 – Ogata Masanori in Taiwan finds plague bacteria in rat fleas; india: 1898 – Simond in Karachi shows transmission by rat fleas; 1905–1908 Indian Plague Commission confirms it; europe: 1347–1353 – Black Death; contemporaries note that it follows ships, goods and clothing but not why; global: 2018 – modelling study (Dean et al.) argues for human ectoparasites in the medieval pandemics; still disputed
- Read: Paul-Louis Simond, La propagation de la peste, Annales de l'Institut Pasteur (1898) | Frank M. Snowden, Epidemics and Society: From the Black Death to the Present (2019) | Katharine R. Dean et al., Human ectoparasites and the spread of plague in Europe during the Second Pandemic, PNAS (2018)

## Typhus carried by body lice (delousing) `typhus_lice`
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, soap, military_camp_hygiene, heat_sterilisation
- Core idea: Epidemic typhus, the fever of armies, jails, ships and famines, is usually spread by body lice. These live and lay their eggs in the seams of clothing and bedding, not on the skin, and the disease enters when their droppings are scratched into the skin. Epidemic typhus can also recur years after the original infection. Delouse everyone in a group on the same day: wash the body with soap, cut or comb the hair, and boil all clothes and bedding for ten minutes, or bake them in an oven at about the heat for bread once the bread is out, or press the seams with a hot iron. Repeat weekly. Clothes left unworn for two to three weeks are free of lice. New arrivals are washed and their clothes baked before they join the others.
- Pitfalls: Washing the person but putting the same clothes back on; the lice are in the seams | Washing clothes in cold or lukewarm water, which lice and eggs survive | Confusing body lice with head lice, or typhus with typhoid | Blaming rats; rat fleas carry the milder murine typhus, not the epidemic kind | Deloused people sharing blankets and straw with those not yet treated
- History: europe: 1489–1490 – first clearly described epidemic, siege of Granada; 1546 Fracastoro separates typhus from plague; 1750s–1760s Pringle and Lind have recruits stripped and washed and their clothes baked, on a theory of infected clothing; 1812 typhus destroys much of Napoleon's army in Russia; africa: 1909 – Nicolle in Tunis proves transmission by the body louse (patients stop infecting others once washed and reclothed); global: 1915 Serbia and 1918–1922 Russia – millions of cases; 1930s Weigl and Cox vaccines; 1943–1944 DDT dusting ends the Naples epidemic
- Read: Charles Nicolle, C. Comte and E. Conseil, Transmission expérimentale du typhus exanthématique par le pou du corps, Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences (1909) | Hans Zinsser, Rats, Lice and History (1935)

## Malaria carried by mosquitoes (drainage, nets) `malaria_mosquito`
- Deps: helped by microscope, contagion_theory, quinine
- Core idea: The recurring fevers of marshy country are caused by a parasite in the blood that usually reaches people through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. They breed in still, fairly clean water (pools, ditches, hoof prints, rice fields) and bite from dusk to dawn. Drain or fill standing water within a kilometre or so of houses, stock ponds with small fish that eat the larvae, pour a film of oil on puddles, sleep under a fine net tucked in on all sides, and build on dry high ground away from marsh. Yellow fever is carried the same way by a different mosquito that breeds in water jars and barrels around houses.
- Pitfalls: Keeping the bad-air theory: closing windows at night helps only if it keeps mosquitoes out | Thinking malaria passes directly from person to person, or from drinking marsh water | Draining the big swamp and ignoring puddles, ditches and borrow pits near the houses | A net with holes or one that is not tucked in | Expecting one fever to give lasting immunity; malaria relapses and can be caught again
- History: egypt: 5th c. BC – Herodotus reports people in the Egyptian marshes sleeping under their fishing nets against gnats; rome: 1st c. BC–1st c. AD – Varro and Columella advise against building near marshes; india: 1897 – Ronald Ross at Secunderabad finds the parasite in an Anopheles mosquito; 1898 works out the full cycle in birds at Calcutta; africa: 1880 – Laveran sees the parasite in blood at Constantine, Algeria; europe: 1717 – Lancisi suspects marsh insects; 1898 Grassi and colleagues in Rome demonstrate transmission of human malaria by Anopheles; americas: 1881 – Finlay in Havana proposes mosquito transmission of yellow fever; 1900 Reed's commission proves it; 1904–1914 Gorgas clears the Panama Canal zone
- Read: Ronald Ross, On some peculiar pigmented cells found in two mosquitos fed on malarial blood, British Medical Journal (1897) | Randall M. Packard, The Making of a Tropical Disease: A Short History of Malaria (2007) | Sonia Shah, The Fever: How Malaria Has Ruled Humankind for 500,000 Years (2010)

## Cinchona bark (quinine) against malaria `quinine`
- Deps: helped by malaria_mosquito, distillation, world_geography
- Core idea: Cinchona bark from Andean cloud forests contains quinine and related alkaloids that act on the blood stages of malaria parasites. Historically the dried bark was powdered and given for intermittent fevers. Bark from different trees varied greatly in strength, so a weight of bark could not specify the dose. Isolation of quinine made measured treatment possible. Ringing ears, nausea and hearing changes are adverse effects and cannot establish that treatment is adequate. Some malaria parasites have dormant liver stages that quinine does not clear.
- Pitfalls: Expecting to find the tree in Europe, Asia or Africa before the 1850s; seeds had to be smuggled from South America | Using it for every fever; it does nothing for plague, typhus or typhoid | Confusing it with willow bark, which is bitter and lowers fever a little but does not cure malaria | Repeating the Countess of Chinchón story, a 17th-century legend; so is the idea that tonic water is a useful dose | Overdose: deafness, blindness, heart failure
- History: americas: c. 1630 – Jesuits in Peru (Lima, Loja) learn of the bark; whether Andean peoples used it against fever before the Spanish is uncertain, as malaria probably arrived with them; europe: 1640s – bark reaches Rome ('Jesuits' powder'); 1670s Talbor's secret remedy; 1712 Torti defines which fevers it cures; 1820 Pelletier and Caventou isolate quinine; china: c. 340 – Ge Hong recommends qinghao (Artemisia annua) soaked in cold water and wrung out for intermittent fevers; 1693 Jesuits cure the Kangxi emperor with cinchona; 1972 Tu Youyou's group isolates artemisinin; india: 1860s – British cinchona plantations (Nilgiris, Darjeeling) from Markham's seeds; east_asia: 1865 onward – Ledger's high-yield seeds grown by the Dutch in Java, which dominates world supply by 1900; africa: 1854 – Baikie's Niger expedition takes quinine daily and loses no one to fever
- Read: Fiammetta Rocco, The Miraculous Fever-Tree: Malaria, Medicine and the Cure that Changed the World (2003) | Saul Jarcho, Quinine's Predecessor: Francesco Torti and the Early History of Cinchona (1993) | Youyou Tu, The discovery of artemisinin (qinghaosu) and gifts from Chinese medicine, Nature Medicine (2011)

## Consumption (tuberculosis) is contagious `tuberculosis_control`
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, microscope, pasteurisation, xrays
- Core idea: Consumption, the slow wasting cough that killed about one adult in five in European cities around 1800, is neither inherited nor a matter of temperament. It is caught by breathing what the sick cough out, mostly over months in crowded, closed, dark rooms, and children catch a form in glands and bones from the milk of sick cows. So: the cougher sleeps alone, coughs into a cloth that is boiled and spits into a pot that is emptied into the fire; rooms are aired and sunned; milk is boiled; nobody with a long cough nurses children or handles food. Rest and good food help the body hold the disease but cure nothing; real cures came with streptomycin and later drugs, taken for many months.
- Pitfalls: Calling it hereditary because it runs in households; that is contagion among people who share a room | Romantic ideas of consumption as a disease of sensitive souls; the royal touch for scrofula | Believing raw milk is healthier; bovine tuberculosis was a major killer of children | Promising a cure: mountain air, sanatoria and Koch's tuberculin (1890) did not cure | Stopping treatment when the patient feels better, which breeds resistant disease
- History: egypt: c. 3000–1000 BC – spinal tuberculosis in mummies; americas: c. AD 1000 – tuberculosis in Peruvian mummies, long before European contact; 1943–1944 streptomycin reported by Schatz, Bugie and Waksman at Rutgers; islamic: 1025 – Ibn Sina's Canon treats phthisis as contagious; europe: 1546 – Fracastoro lists phthisis among contagions; 1699 Lucca and 1782 Naples order reporting and disinfection; 1865 Villemin transmits it to rabbits; 1882 Koch finds the bacillus; 1921 BCG vaccine (Calmette and Guérin); 1948 British streptomycin trial, a landmark randomised trial with concealed allocation
- Read: Robert Koch, Die Aetiologie der Tuberculose, Berliner klinische Wochenschrift (1882) | Thomas Dormandy, The White Death: A History of Tuberculosis (1999) | Helen Bynum, Spitting Blood: The History of Tuberculosis (2012)

## Parasitic worms (hookworm, roundworm, tapeworm, guinea worm) `parasitic_worms`
- Deps: helped by sanitation_sewerage, food_hygiene, microscope, spontaneous_generation_refuted
- Core idea: Worms in the body do not arise there; each comes from eggs or larvae that entered by a known door. Hookworm larvae hatch in soil fouled with excrement and bore through bare feet, causing the pale, weak, 'lazy' sickness of warm farming country: latrines and shoes end it. Roundworm and whipworm eggs are swallowed with soil, unwashed vegetables and dirty fingers. Beef and pork can transmit different tapeworms; pork and wild game can carry Trichinella. Meat colour alone cannot establish a safe cooking temperature. Guinea worm comes from swallowing tiny water fleas: strain drinking water through tightly woven cloth and keep people with an emerging worm out of the pond. Blood flukes enter the skin when wading in still water with snails.
- Pitfalls: Believing worms are generated by rotting food, bad humours or sweets inside the gut | Purging the worms out while people go on walking barefoot on fouled ground | Assuming smoking, salting or brief frying makes pork safe | Thinking this is only a tropical problem; medieval and Roman European latrines are full of worm eggs
- History: egypt: c. 1550 BC – Ebers papyrus describes worms and remedies; blood-fluke eggs found in mummies; 1851 Bilharz discovers the blood fluke in Cairo; 1898 Looss shows hookworm larvae enter through the skin; china: c. 168 BC – body of Lady Dai (Mawangdui) contains whipworm, pinworm and blood-fluke eggs; islamic: 1025 – Ibn Sina's Canon distinguishes several kinds of intestinal worm; europe: 1668–1684 – Redi shows parasites come from eggs; 1855 Küchenmeister demonstrates the tapeworm life cycle; 1860 Zenker links trichina in pork to human disease; 1880 hookworm anaemia among Gotthard tunnel workers; americas: 1909–1914 – Rockefeller Sanitary Commission campaign against hookworm in the US South
- Read: F. E. G. Cox, History of human parasitology, Clinical Microbiology Reviews (2002) | John Ettling, The Germ of Laziness: Rockefeller Philanthropy and Public Health in the New South (1981)

## Fresh food prevents scurvy (citrus, vitamin C) `scurvy_citrus`
- Deps: helped by controlled_trial, vitamins_deficiency
- Core idea: Scurvy (bleeding gums, old wounds reopening, exhaustion, death) appears after six weeks to three months without fresh food and is not catching. The body needs a small daily amount of a substance found in fresh fruit and vegetables and in fresh, lightly cooked meat. The juice of one lemon or orange a day prevents and cures it within a week or two. The substance is destroyed by boiling down, long storage, air and copper vessels, so use fresh juice or juice preserved cold with spirit, sprouted beans or peas, sauerkraut, fresh potatoes, or a tea of fresh pine or spruce needles steeped, not boiled.
- Pitfalls: Preserving the juice by boiling it down to a syrup, which is why Lind's own 'rob' failed | Thinking sourness is what cures and substituting vinegar or acid, as navies did | Assuming all citrus is equal: West Indian limes hold far less than lemons, and scurvy returned to British ships and polar expeditions after 1860 | Blaming idleness, damp, salt meat or bad air, or treating it as contagious | Saying Lind's trial ended scurvy; the navy took 40 years to act, and Lind himself stayed unsure of the cause
- History: americas: 1536 – St Lawrence Iroquoians cure Cartier's crew with a decoction of a conifer ('annedda', probably white cedar); europe: 1601 – Lancaster gives lemon juice on an East India voyage; 1617 Woodall's Surgions Mate recommends it; 1747 Lind's comparative trial on HMS Salisbury (published 1753); 1795 Royal Navy issues lemon juice; 1907 Holst and Frølich produce scurvy in guinea pigs; 1928–1932 Szent-Györgyi and King isolate vitamin C
- Read: James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753) | Kenneth J. Carpenter, The History of Scurvy and Vitamin C (1986) | Stephen R. Bown, Scurvy: How a Surgeon, a Mariner, and a Gentleman Solved the Greatest Medical Mystery of the Age of Sail (2003)

## Deficiency diseases (beriberi, rickets, pellagra, goitre, night blindness) `vitamins_deficiency`
- Deps: helped by controlled_trial, scurvy_citrus, nixtamalisation, epidemiology_mapping
- Core idea: Some diseases come from something missing in the food, not from a germ or a poison. Replacing the missing nutrient can reverse some symptoms; severe or longstanding deficiency can leave permanent damage. Beriberi (weak legs, heart failure) strikes people living on polished white rice: eat unpolished rice, the bran, beans or meat. Rickets (bent bones in children) can result from a shortage of vitamin D or calcium; limited sunlight increases the risk of vitamin D deficiency. Pellagra (rough skin, diarrhoea, madness) follows a diet of maize that was not treated with lime: add meat, milk, beans, or prepare maize the Mesoamerican way. Iodine deficiency can cause goitre and impair fetal brain development; iodised salt helps prevent it. Vitamin A deficiency is one cause of night blindness; vitamin A-rich foods help prevent that deficiency.
- Pitfalls: Looking for a germ or a spoiled-food poison; this delayed the answer to beriberi and pellagra by decades | Giving more of the same poor food instead of a different food | Sunning children behind glass or fully clothed, which does nothing against rickets | Overdosing: too much liver or fish-liver oil poisons, and iodine doses must be tiny | Presenting vitamins as a cure for diseases in well-fed people
- History: egypt: c. 1550 BC – Ebers papyrus prescribes liver for an eye disease usually read as night blindness; china: c. 340 – Ge Hong recommends seaweed for goitre; 7th c. Sun Simiao describes beriberi and treats goitre with animal thyroid and seaweed; americas: from c. 1500 BC – lime treatment of maize protects Mesoamerican peoples from pellagra; 1914–1915 Goldberger proves pellagra dietary; 1924 iodised salt in Michigan; 1937 Elvehjem identifies niacin; east_asia: 1884 – Takaki Kanehiro ends beriberi in the Japanese navy by changing the ration; 1897 Eijkman (Batavia) produces it in chickens fed polished rice; 1901 Grijns reads it as a deficiency; europe: 1650 – Glisson describes rickets; 1735 Casal describes pellagra in Spain; 1820 Coindet treats goitre with iodine; 1912 Hopkins and Funk state the vitamin idea; 1919–1922 Mellanby, Huldschinsky and Chick show cod-liver oil and light cure rickets; 1922 iodised salt in Switzerland
- Read: Casimir Funk, The etiology of the deficiency diseases, Journal of State Medicine (1912) | Joseph Goldberger, The Etiology of Pellagra: The Significance of Certain Epidemiological Observations with Respect Thereto, Public Health Reports (1914) | Kenneth J. Carpenter, Beriberi, White Rice, and Vitamin B (2000)

## Variolation (inoculation with smallpox matter) `variolation`
- Deps: helped by quarantine, probability_statistics
- Core idea: Variolation deliberately exposed people to smallpox. Survivors generally gained lasting protection, but the infection could be severe or fatal and could spread to others until the last scab fell. The Boston records of 1721 reported roughly two deaths per hundred inoculated people, against about fourteen per hundred recorded natural cases. The groups were not randomly assigned, so the comparison supports a lower risk without establishing its exact size. Vaccination later offered protection without giving the recipient smallpox.
- Pitfalls: Not isolating the inoculated, who then start an epidemic among the unprotected | Deep cuts, large doses and weeks of bleeding and purging as 'preparation', which raised the death rate in early European practice | Assuming a mild case in one person predicts a mild infection in another | Calling it safe; it kills some people, which must be said beforehand | Confusing it with vaccination, which uses cowpox and cannot spread smallpox
- History: china: c. 1549 – first reliable mention (Wan Quan); widespread nasal insufflation by the 17th c.; stories of an 11th-century origin are legend; india: 18th c. – inoculation by travelling practitioners documented in Bengal (Holwell 1767); claims of great antiquity rest on weak evidence; africa: before 1700 – practised in parts of West and North Africa; c. 1706 the enslaved African Onesimus describes it to Cotton Mather in Boston; islamic: by c. 1700 – folk practice in the Ottoman lands; 1714 Timoni reports the practice from Constantinople; Pylarini publishes his account in 1715; europe: 1721 – Lady Mary Wortley Montagu has her daughter inoculated in London; 1760s Sutton's light method makes it routine; americas: 1721 – Boylston inoculates about 240 people in Boston: about 2 % die against 14 % of natural cases
- Read: Zabdiel Boylston, An Historical Account of the Small-Pox Inoculated in New England (1726) | Arthur Boylston, The origins of inoculation, Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine (2012) | Donald R. Hopkins, The Greatest Killer: Smallpox in History (2002)

## Smallpox vaccination with cowpox `smallpox_vaccination`
- Deps: helped by variolation, contagion_theory, controlled_trial
- Core idea: Exposure to a related orthopoxvirus can train the immune system to recognise smallpox without causing smallpox itself. Jenner used material associated with cowpox; later campaigns used vaccinia. Early programmes relayed vaccine from person to person because activity could be lost during a long journey. That practice could also transmit unrelated infections. Local vaccine reactions were expected, protection could wane, and repeat vaccination was used. Reliable vaccine supplies, case finding and vaccination of contacts were central to eradication.
- Pitfalls: Expecting to find cowpox on any farm; it is rare and sporadic, and most sores on udders are something else and give no protection | Passing syphilis or other disease arm to arm; even apparently healthy donors could carry infection | Believing one vaccination protects for life | Letting the vaccine die out; without a chain of fresh arms or careful drying it is lost | Telling the milkmaid story as Jenner's flash of insight; the observation was country knowledge, and the farmer Benjamin Jesty vaccinated his family in 1774
- History: europe: 1774 – Jesty (Dorset) inoculates his family with cowpox; 1796 Jenner vaccinates James Phipps and tests him with smallpox; 1798 publication; islamic: 1800–1801 – vaccine sent from Vienna via Constantinople and Baghdad towards India; india: 1802 – first vaccinations in Bombay; americas: 1800 – Waterhouse vaccinates in Boston; 1803–1806 the Spanish Balmis expedition carries vaccine arm to arm through orphan boys to Spanish America and the Philippines; china: 1805 – vaccination reaches Macau and Canton; global: 1980 – WHO declares smallpox eradicated; the vaccine strain (vaccinia) turned out to be closer to horsepox than to cowpox
- Read: Edward Jenner, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae (1798) | Donald R. Hopkins, The Greatest Killer: Smallpox in History (2002)

## Vaccines from weakened or killed germs `vaccines_attenuated`
- Deps: needs contagion_theory, microorganisms; helped by smallpox_vaccination, heat_sterilisation, controlled_trial
- Core idea: Vaccination exposes the immune system to an antigen so that later exposure triggers a faster protective response. Live attenuated vaccines use a weakened organism, inactivated vaccines use a non-replicating preparation, and toxoids train the body to neutralise a bacterial toxin. Each requires evidence of safety, potency and protection. Antitoxin serum serves a different purpose and does not train the immune system. The distinction matters when judging what Pasteur’s vaccine demonstrations established.
- Pitfalls: Trying this without pure cultures and animal tests; an under-weakened culture gives the disease | Contaminated or mislabelled batches (Lübeck 1930: 72 infants died of a BCG lot mixed with virulent tuberculosis) | Expecting instant protection, or one vaccine for all diseases | Taking Pasteur's published account at face value; his notebooks show the anthrax vaccine was made by a rival's chemical method and the rabies treatment was barely tested
- History: europe: 1879–1880 – Pasteur weakens chicken cholera; 1881 anthrax trial at Pouilly-le-Fort; 1885 rabies treatment of Joseph Meister; 1896 Wright and Pfeiffer, killed typhoid vaccine; 1921 BCG; 1923 Ramon's diphtheria toxoid; americas: 1937 – Theiler's yellow fever vaccine; 1955 Salk's polio vaccine after a trial with 1.8 million children
- Read: Louis Pasteur, De l’atténuation du choléra des poules, Recueil de médecine vétérinaire (1880) | Gerald L. Geison, The Private Science of Louis Pasteur (1995)

## Antitoxin serum (passive immunisation) `antitoxin_serum`
- Deps: needs contagion_theory, microorganisms; helped by vaccines_attenuated, controlled_trial
- Core idea: Antitoxin serum supplies ready-made antibodies that act promptly but wear off. It serves a different purpose from a vaccine, which exposes the immune system to an antigen so that the body builds its own protection. The distinction matters when judging what Behring and Kitasato’s serum experiments established.
- Pitfalls: Horse serum given twice can cause severe allergic shock | Expecting lasting protection; the supplied antibodies wear off | Calling serum a vaccine; it supplies antibodies and does not train the immune system
- History: europe: 1890 – Behring and Kitasato, tetanus and diphtheria antitoxin
- Read: Emil Behring and Shibasaburo Kitasato, Ueber das Zustandekommen der Diphtherie-Immunität und der Tetanus-Immunität bei Thieren, Deutsche medizinische Wochenschrift (1890)

## Wound care (stop bleeding, clean, tie vessels, leave dirty wounds open) `wound_care`
- Deps: helped by heat_sterilisation, antiseptics, hand_hygiene, blood_circulation, anatomy_dissection
- Core idea: Use firm, continuous direct pressure to control bleeding and obtain urgent help for severe blood loss. Clean minor wounds with ample clean water and cover with a clean dressing. Deep, heavily contaminated or crushed wounds need skilled exploration and removal of dead tissue. Whether and when to close a wound depends on its condition, site and infection risk; a universal six-hour cut-off is unreliable. Leave embedded objects in place for skilled removal. Spreading redness, fever or pus warrants assessment. Ligatures, drainage and sutures were important surgical advances but each requires the appropriate skills and clean equipment.
- Pitfalls: Cautery with hot iron or boiling oil, and pouring irritants into the wound | Sewing a dirty or deep stab wound shut, which breeds gangrene and lockjaw | Believing 'laudable pus' is needed for healing and provoking it | Dressings of cobweb, dung, earth or unwashed rags (tetanus) | A tourniquet left on for hours, or tied too loosely so that it only blocks the veins
- History: egypt: c. 1600 BC – Edwin Smith papyrus: stitching, splints, honey and grease on wounds; india: early centuries AD – Sushruta Samhita: sutures, drainage, reconstruction of the nose (dating disputed); rome: 1st c. AD – Celsus describes tying bleeding vessels and the signs of inflammation; islamic: c. 1000 – al-Zahrawi (Córdoba) illustrates instruments, gut sutures and ligatures; europe: 1267 – Theodoric of Lucca argues wounds should heal clean without pus; 1545 Paré replaces boiling oil with a mild dressing; 1564 Paré ties arteries in amputations; 1718 Petit's screw tourniquet; 1898 Friedrich studies early excision in experimental wounds; this did not establish a universal six-hour limit
- Read: Ambroise Paré, La méthode de traicter les playes faictes par hacquebutes et aultres bastons à feu (1545) | Guido Majno, The Healing Hand: Man and Wound in the Ancient World (1975)

## Antiseptics (strong spirit, chlorinated lime, carbolic acid, iodine) `antiseptics`
- Deps: helped by distillation, contagion_theory, chlorine_bleach, hand_hygiene, heat_sterilisation
- Core idea: Antiseptics reduce microbes on living skin. Suitable alcohol-based preparations disinfect intact skin; wine is too dilute, and neither alcohol nor a quick chemical dip sterilises surgical instruments. Clean instruments first, then use a validated sterilisation process. Wash dirt from minor wounds with clean water. Chlorinated lime, phenol and iodine preparations belong to different periods of antisepsis and have different uses and hazards. Lister used carbolic acid in dressings and on equipment; strong phenol can damage tissue, and the smell of chlorine cannot determine a safe dilution.
- Pitfalls: Using wine, beer or ordinary brandy and believing it sterilises | Thinking pure spirit is better than diluted; about 70 % works best, and no spirit kills the spores of lockjaw and gangrene | Flooding open wounds with strong carbolic or sublimate, which kills tissue and can poison | Dipping dirty instruments briefly instead of cleaning them first | Spirit near a flame or cautery
- History: egypt: c. 1600 BC – honey and resins on wounds (Edwin Smith papyrus); greece: c. 400 BC – Hippocratic texts wash wounds with wine and vinegar; europe: 1267 – Theodoric of Lucca uses wine-soaked dressings; 1820s Labarraque's chlorine solutions; 1847 Semmelweis; 1867 Lister's carbolic acid method for compound fractures; 1881 Koch tests disinfectants on bacteria; 1908 Grossich's iodine skin preparation; 1915 Dakin's dilute hypochlorite for war wounds
- Read: Joseph Lister, On the antiseptic principle in the practice of surgery, British Medical Journal (1867) | Lindsey Fitzharris, The Butchering Art (2017) | Guido Majno, The Healing Hand: Man and Wound in the Ancient World (1975)

## Sterilising instruments and dressings by heat `heat_sterilisation`
- Deps: helped by contagion_theory, spontaneous_generation_refuted, safety_valve_boiler, antiseptics
- Core idea: Cleaning removes blood and debris that shield microbes. Boiling reduces infection risk but can leave bacterial spores alive. Sterilising surgical instruments requires a validated process. Saturated steam must contact every surface after air is removed; a gravity-displacement steriliser typically exposes wrapped instruments to 121 °C for 30 minutes once the load reaches temperature. The required cycle depends on the load and the equipment. Check cycle indicators, dry the packs and protect them from contamination until use. Repeated boiling is unreliable for instruments.
- Pitfalls: Sterilising the knife and then laying it on the table, wiping it on an apron or handling it with unwashed fingers | Dipping instruments in hot water for a moment | Boiling without first cleaning off dried blood and pus | Assuming boiling kills everything; spores survive, which is why Tyndall and Pasteur's opponents got growth in boiled hay broth | A sealed pressure vessel without a safety valve
- History: europe: 1760s – Spallanzani shows long boiling in sealed flasks prevents growth; 1810 Appert preserves food by heat; 1877 Tyndall finds heat-resistant spores; 1879 Chamberland's autoclave; 1881 Koch, Gaffky and Loeffler show steam beats dry heat and chemicals; 1886 von Bergmann introduces steam-sterilised dressings; 1891–1892 Schimmelbusch's system of asepsis; americas: c. 1890 – Halsted introduces rubber gloves at Johns Hopkins
- Read: Robert Koch, Georg Gaffky and Friedrich Loeffler, Versuche über die Verwerthbarkeit heisser Wasserdämpfe zu Desinfectionszwecken, Mittheilungen aus dem Kaiserlichen Gesundheitsamte (1881) | Curt Schimmelbusch, Anleitung zur aseptischen Wundbehandlung (1892) | Thomas Schlich, Asepsis and bacteriology: a realignment of surgery and laboratory science, Medical History (2012)

## Safe childbirth (clean hands, patience, cord care, forceps) `childbirth_care`
- Deps: helped by hand_hygiene, heat_sterilisation, antiseptics, anatomy_dissection
- Core idea: Childbed fever, the great killer of new mothers, is carried into the womb by the hands and instruments of attendants who come from corpses, wounds or other sick women. So: clean hands, sterile instruments and clean linen, as few internal examinations as possible, and nobody attends a birth after a dissection or a fever case. Let labour take its time. Tie the cord in two places with boiled thread and cut between with a boiled blade; put nothing on the stump. Dry the child, keep it warm on the mother's skin and let it suck at once, first milk included. Do not pull on the cord; rub the womb through the belly if bleeding continues. Obstetric forceps, two curved blades that lock around the head, can deliver a stuck child alive.
- Pitfalls: Assuming physicians and hospitals were safer than midwives; before 1880 lying-in hospitals had the highest death rates | Dressing the cord stump with dung, earth, ash or butter, the cause of lockjaw in newborns | Throwing away the first milk and giving the newborn honey, wine or water instead | Pulling on the cord or hurrying labour with ergot before the child is born, which can tear the womb | Treating a single successful caesarean as evidence of low risk; haemorrhage and infection killed many mothers
- History: rome: 2nd c. AD – Soranus of Ephesus writes a midwifery manual with clean, gentle practice and turning the child; islamic: c. 1000 – al-Zahrawi describes obstetric instruments and positions; china: 1715 – Dasheng bian advises patience and minimal interference: 'sleep, bear the pain, delay approaching the tub'; europe: 1549 – Paré revives turning the child by the feet; c. 1600–1730 the Chamberlen family keeps the forceps secret; 1752 Smellie's midwifery; 1759 du Coudray trains French midwives with a mannequin; 1795 Gordon, 1843 Holmes, 1847 Semmelweis on childbed fever; 1879 Pasteur identifies the streptococcus; africa: 1879 – in Bunyoro, present-day Uganda, Felkin witnesses a local surgeon deliver a baby by caesarean section; mother and baby survive in his account, published in 1884
- Read: Ignaz Semmelweis, Die Aetiologie, der Begriff und die Prophylaxis des Kindbettfiebers (1861) | Irvine Loudon, The Tragedy of Childbed Fever (2000) | Soranus, Soranus’ Gynecology (tr. Owsei Temkin, 1956) | Robert W. Felkin, Notes on Labour in Central Africa, Transactions of the Edinburgh Obstetrical Society (1884)

## First aid and resuscitation `first_aid_resuscitation`
- Deps: helped by blood_circulation, wound_care
- Core idea: Get help and check breathing. For an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally or is only gasping, start chest compressions in the centre of the chest, 100–120 per minute, about 5–6 cm deep, letting the chest rise fully. Use a defibrillator as soon as available. A trained rescuer provides two breaths for every thirty compressions; rescue breaths are especially important after drowning. Place an unconscious person who is breathing normally on their side and keep checking breathing. Apply firm direct pressure to severe bleeding. Cool a burn with clean running water for twenty minutes and cover it.
- Pitfalls: Period methods for the drowned: hanging by the feet, rolling over a barrel, blowing tobacco smoke into the bowel | Pouring drink into the mouth of an unconscious person | Butter, oil, flour or dung on burns | Forcing something between the teeth of someone in a fit | Promising that chest compression revives the dead; without a defibrillator most cardiac arrests stay fatal
- History: europe: 1732 – Tossach revives a suffocated miner by mouth-to-mouth breathing (published 1744); 1767 Amsterdam society for rescuing the drowned; 1774 Royal Humane Society, London; 1790s Larrey's flying ambulances and sorting of the wounded by urgency; 1863 Red Cross; 1877–1882 St John Ambulance and Esmarch's first-aid courses for laymen; americas: 1958 – Safar and Elam prove mouth-to-mouth beats the arm-lift methods; 1960 Kouwenhoven, Jude and Knickerbocker introduce closed-chest compression; 1974 Heimlich's abdominal thrust
- Read: Peter Safar, Lourdes A. Escarraga and James O. Elam, A comparison of the mouth-to-mouth and mouth-to-airway methods of artificial respiration with the chest-pressure arm-lift methods, New England Journal of Medicine (1958) | W. B. Kouwenhoven, James R. Jude and G. Guy Knickerbocker, Closed-chest cardiac massage, Journal of the American Medical Association (1960) | Mickey S. Eisenberg, Life in the Balance: Emergency Medicine and the Quest to Reverse Sudden Death (1997)

## Ether anaesthesia `ether_anaesthesia`
- Deps: needs distillation, sulphuric_acid; helped by heat_sterilisation, antiseptics
- Core idea: Ether vapour can produce general anaesthesia, allowing surgery that would otherwise be unbearably painful. The depth of anaesthesia depends on the concentration inhaled and the patient’s breathing. Loss of consciousness can also mean loss of protective airway reflexes, airway obstruction or stopped breathing. Historical open-drop administration gave poor control of concentration. A trained attendant must manage the airway and ventilation throughout induction, surgery and recovery. Ether is highly flammable, and its dense vapour can travel along floors to a distant ignition source.
- Pitfalls: Candles, lamps, fire or cautery in the room | Pouring on too much or leaving the cloth on when breathing weakens; nobody assigned to watch | A full stomach: the patient vomits and breathes it in | Crude ether still containing acid, or old ether kept in light and air, which forms explosive residues | Believing painless surgery is safe surgery; without clean hands and instruments more operations meant more deaths from infection
- History: china: c. AD 200 – Hua Tuo said to operate under a drug called mafeisan; recipe lost, account semi-legendary; east_asia: 1804 – Hanaoka Seishu (Japan) removes a breast tumour under a herbal general anaesthetic (tsusensan); europe: 1540 – Valerius Cordus describes making 'sweet oil of vitriol'; Paracelsus notes it puts chickens to sleep; 1800 Davy suggests nitrous oxide for surgery; 1847 Simpson introduces chloroform; americas: 1842 – Crawford Long (Georgia) operates under ether, unpublished until 1849; 1844 Wells tries nitrous oxide for dentistry; 16 October 1846 Morton's public demonstration in Boston
- Read: Thomas Dormandy, The Worst of Evils: The Fight Against Pain (2006) | Stephanie J. Snow, Blessed Days of Anaesthesia: How Anaesthetics Changed the World (2008)

## Pain relief with opium and willow bark (laudanum, morphine, aspirin) `opium_analgesia`
- Deps: helped by distillation, synthetic_dyes
- Core idea: Opium is dried poppy latex containing morphine and other alkaloids. It can relieve severe pain, but the same drugs can suppress breathing and cause fatal overdose. Laudanum was a historical tincture; neither a drop count nor appearance establishes the strength of a homemade preparation. Alcohol adds to respiratory depression. Repeated use can cause tolerance and physical dependence, and withdrawal can follow abrupt cessation. Willow bark contains salicylates, which act differently. Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, a manufactured drug that can also cause bleeding.
- Pitfalls: Dosing opium by guess; the gap between relief and death is small, and smaller with wine | Laudanum to quieten babies, which killed many children | Calling willow bark 'natural aspirin' and expecting tablet strength; a cup of bark tea holds very little | Giving aspirin-like drugs to bleeding patients | Repeating that ancient Egyptians and Hippocrates used willow as a painkiller; the textual evidence is thin
- History: mesopotamia: c. 3000 BC – a Sumerian sign often read as 'joy plant' may mean the poppy (disputed); egypt: c. 1550 BC – Ebers papyrus: poppy remedy to stop children crying; greece: 1st c. AD – Dioscorides describes how to score poppy capsules and collect opium, and warns of overdose; islamic: 1025 – Ibn Sina's Canon gives opium's uses and dangers; Arab traders carry it east; china: 7th–8th c. – poppy known as medicine; opium smoking spreads in the 17th–18th c.; europe: 1660s – Sydenham's laudanum; 1763 Edward Stone reports willow bark for agues; 1804–1817 Sertürner isolates morphine; 1828 salicin; 1853 hypodermic syringe (Pravaz, Wood); 1897–1899 aspirin at Bayer (credit disputed between Hoffmann and Eichengrün)
- Read: Friedrich Sertürner, Ueber das Morphium, eine neue salzfähige Grundlage, und die Mekonsäure, Annalen der Physik (1817) | Martin Booth, Opium: A History (1996) | Diarmuid Jeffreys, Aspirin: The Remarkable Story of a Wonder Drug (2004)

## Blood groups and transfusion `blood_groups_transfusion`
- Deps: helped by blood_circulation, heat_sterilisation, microscope, refrigeration
- Core idea: Donor red cells carry antigens that a recipient’s antibodies may attack, causing potentially fatal haemolysis. ABO and RhD typing, an antibody screen and compatibility testing guide selection. Visible clumping reveals some mismatches, but a negative bedside slide test does not establish compatibility. Group O red cells lack A and B antigens; group O whole blood also contains donor plasma whose antibodies may attack the recipient’s cells. Citrate prevents clotting, while sterile collection, donor screening and controlled cold storage address separate hazards. Sterile intravenous crystalloid can restore volume but cannot carry oxygen.
- Pitfalls: Animal blood (the lamb's blood transfusions of 1667 ended in deaths and a ban) | Assuming relatives always match | Skipping the test in an emergency | Passing on syphilis, malaria or jaundice from the donor | Air in the tubing, or running blood in too fast
- History: europe: 1665 – Lower transfuses dog to dog; 1667 Denis gives lamb's blood to a man; banned c. 1670; 1818–1829 Blundell's human-to-human transfusions for bleeding after childbirth; 1832 Latta's saline infusion in cholera; 1901 Landsteiner's blood groups (Vienna); 1902 fourth group (Decastello, Sturli); 1914 citrate (Hustin, Brussels); 1917 Robertson establishes stored-blood depots on the Western Front; americas: 1907 – Ottenberg cross-matches before transfusing; 1914–1915 citrate method (Agote in Buenos Aires, Lewisohn in New York); 1937 Fantus's blood bank in Chicago; 1940 Rhesus factor (Landsteiner, Wiener)
- Read: Karl Landsteiner, Ueber Agglutinationserscheinungen normalen menschlichen Blutes, Wiener klinische Wochenschrift (1901) | Douglas Starr, Blood: An Epic History of Medicine and Commerce (1998) | Holly Tucker, Blood Work: A Tale of Medicine and Murder in the Scientific Revolution (2011)

## Human anatomy from dissection `anatomy_dissection`
- Deps: helped by empiricism_over_authority, perspective_technical_drawing, printing_press
- Core idea: What is inside the human body has to be learned by opening human bodies and drawing what is there, not from books. Galen, the authority for 1,300 years, dissected apes, pigs and oxen, and his human anatomy carries their features: a five-lobed liver, a net of vessels at the base of the brain, pores through the wall between the heart's chambers, a lower jaw in two pieces. None exists in man, and anyone can check. The teacher must cut with his own hands in front of the students instead of reading aloud while a barber cuts, and the findings should be printed as accurate pictures by trained artists. Opening the dead after an illness then shows which organ the disease damaged.
- Pitfalls: Claiming the Church forbade dissection; Italian universities held public dissections from about 1300 and the papal bull of 1299 concerned boiling crusaders' bones | Saying Vesalius overthrew Galen; he corrected some 200 points and still kept Galen's physiology | Supposing anatomy immediately improved treatment; it took 300 years | Dissecting and then examining living patients or women in labour with unwashed hands | Half-remembered school anatomy stated as fact (side of the liver, number of ribs, course of vessels) that a local surgeon can refute
- History: egypt: c. 300 BC – Herophilus and Erasistratus dissect human bodies in Alexandria; the practice lapses after them; rome: 2nd c. AD – Galen's anatomy from animals becomes canonical; india: early centuries AD – Sushruta Samhita describes studying a body softened in running water (dating disputed); china: AD 16 – dissection of an executed rebel under Wang Mang; 1045 anatomical drawings from executed rebels (Ou Xifan); 1830 Wang Qingren corrects the classics; islamic: c. 1200 – Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi corrects Galen on the jaw from skeletons in Egypt; no regular dissection; europe: 1316 – Mondino's dissection manual, Bologna; c. 1489–1513 Leonardo's drawings (unpublished); 1543 Vesalius, Fabrica; 1761 Morgagni links symptoms to organ damage found after death; east_asia: 1754 – Yamawaki Toyo observes a dissection in Kyoto; 1774 Kaitai shinsho, a Dutch anatomy translated into Japanese
- Read: Andreas Vesalius, De humani corporis fabrica (1543) | Charles D. O'Malley, Andreas Vesalius of Brussels, 1514–1564 (1964) | Katharine Park, Secrets of Women: Gender, Generation, and the Origins of Human Dissection (2006)

## Circulation of the blood `blood_circulation`
- Deps: helped by anatomy_dissection, piston_pump, microscope, measurement_quantification
- Core idea: The heart is a pump with valves. It drives the same blood round and round: out through the arteries to the body, back through the veins, then through the lungs and out again. Blood is not made afresh in the liver and used up in the flesh. Harvey's proof is arithmetic: if the heart throws out even a small mouthful at each beat, over a thousand beats in half an hour, it moves more blood in an hour than the whole body holds or any meal could supply. The demonstration: tie a band round the upper arm so the veins swell, then press along a vein. The little valves let blood pass only towards the heart. The fine vessels joining arteries to veins are too small to see without a microscope.
- Pitfalls: Saying all arteries carry bright blood and all veins dark; the vessels between heart and lungs are the reverse | Claiming it changed medicine at once; bleeding went on for two more centuries | Crediting Harvey with knowing what the lungs do or seeing capillaries; he did neither | Calling older ideas stupid; Galen's ebb-and-flow system explained a great deal and Harvey kept much of it
- History: china: c. 2nd–1st c. BC – Huangdi neijing speaks of blood and qi flowing in an endless circuit; a doctrine, not an anatomical demonstration; islamic: c. 1242 – Ibn al-Nafis (Damascus, Cairo) denies the pores in the heart wall and describes blood passing through the lungs; europe: 1553 Servetus and 1559 Colombo describe the passage through the lungs; 1603 Fabricius describes the valves in veins; 1628 Harvey, De motu cordis; 1661 Malpighi sees capillaries in a frog's lung; 1733 Hales measures blood pressure in a horse
- Read: William Harvey, Exercitatio anatomica de motu cordis et sanguinis in animalibus (1628) | Thomas Wright, Circulation: William Harvey's Revolutionary Idea (2012)

## Physical diagnosis (percussion, stethoscope, thermometer, pulse count) `clinical_thermometer_stethoscope`
- Deps: helped by thermometer_temperature, anatomy_dissection, mechanical_clock, data_graphs
- Core idea: Examine the body instead of only questioning the patient and looking at urine. Tap the chest with a finger: air-filled lung sounds hollow like an empty cask, fluid or solid lung sounds dull. Listen through a wooden tube about 30 cm long with one end on the chest and the other at the ear: breathing, crackles and heart sounds are heard clearly and differ in pneumonia, consumption and heart disease. Count the pulse against a watch (60–100 a minute at rest in an adult) and the breaths (12–20). Measure the temperature with a small mercury thermometer under the tongue or in the armpit for several minutes (normal about 37 °C, within half a degree) and plot it twice daily; the curve tracks the illness but usually cannot identify its cause. Each sign means something in the context of symptoms, other findings and the course of illness. Comparing bedside findings with autopsies helped establish those associations.
- Pitfalls: Expecting the instrument to cure; it only tells diseases apart | Treating fever as the disease itself and fighting the number | Thinking the stethoscope amplifies; it mainly isolates the sound, and an untrained ear hears nothing useful | Using a room thermometer that responds slowly and is read after removal, when it has already fallen | Quoting 37.0 °C as exact; healthy people vary by time of day
- History: egypt: c. 300 BC – Herophilus of Alexandria times the pulse with a water clock; china: c. 280 – Wang Shuhe's Mai jing systematises pulse diagnosis; europe: c. 1612 – Santorio uses a thermoscope on patients; 1707 Floyer's pulse watch; 1761 Auenbrugger (Vienna) describes percussion; 1816–1819 Laennec invents the stethoscope; 1867 Allbutt's short clinical thermometer; 1868 Wunderlich's fever curves from about 25,000 patients; 1896 Riva-Rocci's blood-pressure cuff
- Read: René Laennec, De l'auscultation médiate (1819) | Carl Wunderlich, Das Verhalten der Eigenwärme in Krankheiten (1868) | Stanley Joel Reiser, Medicine and the Reign of Technology (1978)

## Tooth decay and dental care `dental_care`
- Deps: helped by microorganisms
- Core idea: Teeth are not eaten by a worm. Decay is caused by the soft film of bacteria on the teeth, which turns sugar and starch into acid that dissolves the tooth. Rub the film off every tooth surface and along the gums twice a day with a frayed twig or a small bristle brush, clean between the teeth with thread or a pick, and eat sweet things rarely rather than all day long. Both the frequency and total amount of sugar matter. Fluoride helps enamel resist acid attack. Swelling around a painful tooth calls for urgent dental assessment. A spreading infection can threaten the airway.
- Pitfalls: Tooth powders of brick dust, pumice, crushed shell or acid, which whiten by wearing the enamel away | The tooth-worm theory and remedies built on it (henbane smoke) | Believing decay is inevitable with age; it follows sugar, and became common in Europe with cheap sugar after 1600 | Pulling teeth with dirty instruments
- History: mesopotamia: by 1st millennium BC – incantation against the tooth worm (older versions likely); india: c. 7000–5500 BC – drilled teeth at Mehrgarh (Indus region); chewing twigs (neem) prescribed in the classical medical texts; islamic: 7th c. – the miswak chewing stick recommended in prophetic tradition; china: bristle toothbrushes in use by the Song period at the latest; the often-quoted date 1498 is poorly documented; europe: 1728 – Fauchard, Le Chirurgien Dentiste, rejects the tooth worm and blames sugar; c. 1780 Addis sells bristle toothbrushes in London; 1890 W. D. Miller explains decay by acid-forming bacteria; americas: 1945 – water fluoridation trial begins in Grand Rapids, Michigan
- Read: Pierre Fauchard, Le Chirurgien Dentiste, ou Traité des dents (1728) | Willoughby D. Miller, The Micro-organisms of the Human Mouth (1890) | A. Coppa et al., Early Neolithic tradition of dentistry, Nature (2006)

## Sulphonamide drugs `sulphonamides`
- Deps: needs synthetic_dyes, contagion_theory; helped by controlled_trial, microorganisms
- Core idea: Prontosil is a red dye that the body converts to sulphanilamide, a colourless compound. That conversion explains why the drug protected animals despite disappointing early tests in glass dishes. Sulphonamides interfere with bacterial folate synthesis and can arrest the growth of susceptible bacteria. Early successes included treatment of streptococcal childbed fever; later compounds extended the range of treatable infections. Activity depends on the organism and resistance. Kidney injury, severe allergic reactions and unsafe formulations all limited use.
- Pitfalls: Screening candidate drugs only in the test tube; Prontosil does nothing there and works in the animal | Believing it is the dye colour that kills germs | Dissolving the drug in an untested solvent: the American 'Elixir Sulfanilamide' of 1937, made with diethylene glycol, killed over 100 people | Expecting every member of the drug class to treat the same infections, or using an antibacterial drug for a viral illness | Short or low dosing, which bred resistant gonorrhoea within a few years
- History: europe: 1908 – Gelmo (Vienna) synthesises sulphanilamide as a dye intermediate; 1932 Domagk at Bayer finds Prontosil protects mice (published 1935); 1935 Jacques and Thérèse Tréfouël, Nitti and Bovet (Paris) show sulphanilamide is the active part; 1936 Colebrook's trial in childbed fever; 1938 sulphapyridine (M&B 693); americas: 1937 – Elixir Sulfanilamide disaster leads to the US Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act of 1938
- Read: Gerhard Domagk, Ein Beitrag zur Chemotherapie der bakteriellen Infektionen, Deutsche medizinische Wochenschrift (1935) | John E. Lesch, The First Miracle Drugs: How the Sulfa Drugs Transformed Medicine (2007) | Thomas Hager, The Demon Under the Microscope (2006)

## Penicillin (antibiotics from mould) `penicillin`
- Deps: needs microorganisms, heat_sterilisation, contagion_theory; helped by microscope, refrigeration, acids_bases_ph, controlled_trial
- Core idea: Certain Penicillium moulds produce a substance that blocks cell-wall construction in susceptible, growing bacteria. A clear zone around a mould colony demonstrates inhibition; it does not establish purity, dose or safety in a patient. The Oxford team had to recover an unstable substance, measure its activity and obtain enough sterile drug for sustained treatment. Different penicillins differ in their stability in stomach acid. Benefit depends on the infecting organism and its susceptibility. Serious allergy is possible, and mould or crude filtrate cannot substitute for a tested medicine.
- Pitfalls: Putting mouldy bread on a wound or eating it; too little penicillin, the wrong moulds, and some moulds make poisons | Assuming any green mould will do, or that Fleming's 1928 observation was already a medicine; it took a team twelve more years | Expecting it to cure plague, tuberculosis, typhoid, cholera, malaria or virus diseases such as smallpox and influenza | Running out mid-treatment: an early Oxford patient, Albert Alexander, improved and then died in 1941 when the supply ended | Forgetting allergy, which can kill within minutes, and that under-dosing breeds resistant germs
- History: europe: 1870s – Burdon-Sanderson, Lister and Tyndall note that moulds suppress bacteria; 1897 Duchesne's thesis in Lyon; 1928 Fleming (published 1929); 1930 Cecil Paine documents topical treatment of eye infections in Sheffield; 1939–1941 Florey, Chain, Heatley and colleagues develop systemic treatment in Oxford; americas: 1941–1944 – Peoria laboratory and US firms develop deep-tank fermentation, corn-steep liquor and a high-yield strain from a mouldy cantaloupe; enough for the Allied armies by June 1944
- Read: Alexander Fleming, On the antibacterial action of cultures of a Penicillium, with special reference to their use in the isolation of B. influenzae, British Journal of Experimental Pathology (1929) | Eric Lax, The Mould in Dr Florey's Coat (2004) | Robert Bud, Penicillin: Triumph and Tragedy (2007) | M. Wainwright and H. T. Swan, C. G. Paine and the earliest surviving clinical records of penicillin therapy, Medical History (1986)
